caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 418 of 2005
lawyer:
Chowdhury Md. Zahangir, Advocate-on-Record—For the Petitioner.
Not represented—The Respondents.
parties:
Jahir Uddin (Md)  ----- Appellant
Vs.
Rupali Bank Ltd. and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam J: This petition for leave to appeal arises out of the judgment dated 6-7-2004 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2499 of 2003 making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated 29-10-2002 passed by learned District Judge, Bogra in Other Class Appeal No. 30 of 2002 affirming those of dated 27-11-2001 passed by learned Assistant Judge, Dupchachai Court, Bogra in Other Class Suit No. 53 of 1999 decreeing the suit. 

 3. The trial Court, after hearing, decreed the suit on the finding, inter alia, that the plaintiff was dismissed from service after institution of the suit and thereafter the plaint being amended seeking relief against dismissal, the suit is maintainable; in the inquiry report the plaintiff was found to be guilty for negligence of duty and though the defendant bank suffered financial loss because of such negligence of duty but charge framed against the plaintiff does not come within the ambit of misconduct as defined in the Service Regulations; the plaintiff got opportunity to defend himself against the charge of misconduct but against the final show cause notice he did not get any opportunity to defend himself. 

 4. As against that the defendant bank preferred Other Class Appeal No. 30 of 2002 and the learned District Judge, Bogra, after hearing, dismissed the appeal holding that no notice to show cause was issued before suspending the plaintiff and thereby principles of natural justice was violated and the charges leveled against the plaintiff were also not proved. The defendant bank then moved the High Court Division and obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 2499 of 2003 and after hearing, the High Court Division made the Rule absolute holding that on 6-4-1984 the defendant bank was denationalized and was converted into a private bank incorporated under the Companies Act, 1913 and, as such, from that date the relationship between the defendant bank and the plaintiff became that of master and servant and therefore the petitioner is not entitled to get a decree for declaration without any consequential relief. 

 6. As it appears the High Court Division made the Rule absolute holding that admittedly, on and from 6-4-1984 the defendant bank, being denationalized, was converted into a private bank incorporated under the Companies Act, 1994 and, as such, the relationship between the plaintiff-petitioner and the defendant bank became that of master and servant from that date and therefore, the petitioner is not entitled to get a decree for declaration without consequential relief; in the instant case there is no prayer for mandatory injunction for consequential relief; even if there is a prayer for mandatory injunction but that too cannot be granted in view of legal bar under clause (e) of section 56 of the Specific Relief Act which provides that an order of mandatory injunction cannot be granted to prevent the breach of a contract the performance of which could not be specifically enforced; the breach of contract for personal service cannot be restrained by court ordering an employer to retain the employee in the service as it is the prerogative right of the employer to discharge his employee and the Court cannot compel a person against his will to employ any person and the employer bank is liable for damage and compensation in terms of Service Rules and Regulations; the suit is not maintainable as the plaintiff challenged the order of suspension and the final show cause notice but did not challenge the order of dismissal in which the impugned order of suspension and show cause merged and with the order of dismissal the orders of suspension and final show cause became infructuous and in the instant case this issue, which cuts the case at its root, has not been considered at all by the appellate Court below. 

 7. As it appears the principle laid down in 7 BLC (AD) 1 on which the High Court Division relied is applicable in the present case, inasmuch as in the above appeal Haji Md Arab Ali, the respondent No. 1, joined in the service of the then Muslim Commercial Bank Limited in the year 1968 and after liberation of Bangladesh the said bank was nationalised and was named as Rupali Bank and then the respondent No.1 was promoted from time to time and in the year 1981 he was promoted to the post of Senior Principal Officer; then, a departmental proceeding was started against him in the year 1984 and consequently, he was suspended on 18-6-1984; Rupali Bank was denationalised on 6-4-1984 and was incorporated under the Companies Act as a private bank named Rupali Bank Limited; the respondent No. 1 was dismissed from service on 25-5-1987; he filed Title Suit No. 2 on 1989 against Rupali Bank Limited and others for declaring the order of his dismissal from service as illegal and for other consequential reliefs; the trial Court decreed the suit on 12-7-1990 and then Rupali Bank Ltd filed Title Appeal No. 239 of 1990 which after hearing was dismissed. As against that, Rupali Bank obtained Rule in Civil Revision No. 3227 of 1993 but the High Court Division, upon hearing, discharged the Rule. Then leave was granted at the instance of the Rupali Bank Ltd to examine the issue as to whether Rupali Bank Ltd was no longer a statutory organisation but a corporate body and a private bank when the order of dismissal from service was passed and so, whether the relationship between the Bank- employer and the plaintiff-employee was that of a master and servant and, as such, he was not entitled to get the reliefs as prayed for in the plaint. 

 "It is the admitted position that the plaintiff is out of his office consequent to the order of his dismissal from his service and therefore the said decree for permanent injunction cannot be an effective relief if the plaintiff gets the declaratory decree to the effect that his dismissal from service is illegal. Under the circumstances, the plaintiff ought to have prayed for a decree of mandatory injunction under section 55 of the Specific Relief Act, but, as we have already held, clause (e) of section 56 of the Specific Relief Act is a bar to get decree for mandatory injunction in the case of the plaintiff. In view of the legal position as discussed above we need not decide the issue as to whether the dismissal from service in question was illegal, but we must hold that the suit is not maintainable on the ground that a declaratory decree will not be enough and that a decree for mandatory injunction necessary as a consequential relief is barred under the law. We, therefore, find that neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court nor the High Court Division considered this vital issue which cuts at the root resulting the suit being not maintainable as framed. The suit ought to have been dismissed on this issue."
